expectedText:
COMMISSION AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DECLARATION OF PARTIES
This Commission Agreement is entered into between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee, effective October 1, 2026, regarding compensation for services Jordan Lee will render in the position of Account Executive.

THE WRITTEN COMMISSION AGREEMENT REQUIREMENT
Under California law, whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within California and the contemplated method of paying that employee involves commissions, the contract must be in writing and must set forth the method by which the commissions are to be computed and paid. This document reflects that requirement for the compensation arrangement between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within this state and the contemplated method of payment of the employee involves commissions, the contract shall be in writing and shall set forth the method by which the commissions shall be computed and paid."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2751(a) (California Legislative Information text), the core written commission contract requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2751.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 2751(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "COMMISSION"
California law defines "commission wages" as compensation paid to a person for services rendered in the sale of the employer's property or services, based proportionately on the amount or value of that property or those services — the same definition the written-commission-contract requirement itself cross-references. For purposes of that writing requirement specifically, the term "commission" does not include short-term productivity bonuses such as those paid to retail clerks, temporary variable incentive payments that increase (but do not decrease) payment under the written contract, or bonus and profit-sharing plans — unless the employer has offered to pay a fixed percentage of sales or profits as compensation for work performed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "As used in this section, “commissions” has the meaning set forth in Section 204.1. For purposes of this section only, “commission” does not include any of the following: (1) Short-term productivity bonuses such as are paid to retail clerks. (2) Temporary, variable incentive payments that increase, but do not decrease, payment under the written contract. (3) Bonus and profit-sharing plans, unless there has been an offer by the employer to pay a fixed percentage of sales or profits as compensation for work to be performed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2751(c) (California Legislative Information text), what does not count as a commission for the writing requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2751.)
  "Commission wages are compensation paid to any person for services rendered in the sale of such employer's property or services and based proportionately upon the amount or value thereof."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 204.1 (California Legislative Information text), the definition of commission wages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=204.1.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. The borrowed definition sits inside § 204.1, a section whose main operative sentence otherwise sets a payday rule specific to vehicle dealers; the definition and the exclusion list are both expressly scoped ("for purposes of this section only") to the § 2751 writing requirement, not stated as a definition of "commission" for every other purpose in the Labor Code. Section 2752, the section immediately following, was checked directly and returned no codified content — it does not contain a separate exclusion list.

COMMISSION STRUCTURE AND RATE SCHEDULE
The method by which Jordan Lee's commissions are computed and paid is set forth as follows: ☐ 5% of net sales revenue on each closed deal, paid on the next regular payday after the customer's payment is received.

WHEN COMMISSION WAGES MUST BE PAID
Outside a narrow vehicle-dealer-specific rule, California's Labor Code does not set a distinct payday schedule for commission wages as such. Commissions earned by Jordan Lee generally fall under the ordinary rule that wages other than those specifically listed elsewhere in the Labor Code (including vehicle-dealer commissions and wages due on discharge or quitting) are due and payable twice during each calendar month, on regular paydays designated in advance by Acme, Inc. Only for a person employed by a vehicle dealer licensed by the Department of Motor Vehicles does the Labor Code set a distinct commission-specific payday rule: commission wages there are due and payable once during each calendar month, on a day designated in advance by the employer as the regular payday.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "All wages, other than those mentioned in Section 201, 201.3, 202, 204.1, or 204.2, earned by any person in any employment are due and payable twice during each calendar month, on days designated in advance by the employer as the regular paydays."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 204(a) (California Legislative Information text), the general twice-monthly payday rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=204.)
  "Commission wages paid to any person employed by an employer licensed as a vehicle dealer by the Department of Motor Vehicles are due and payable once during each calendar month on a day designated in advance by the employer as the regular payday."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 204.1 (California Legislative Information text), the vehicle-dealer-specific once-monthly commission payday rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=204.1.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. The twice-monthly general payday rule and the once-monthly vehicle-dealer-specific commission payday rule are the only statutory payday-timing rules this research found; there is no separate general "commission wages must be paid within X days of being earned" statute distinct from the ordinary payday rule and the final-pay-on-discharge rule already covered elsewhere in this corpus, which this clause does not re-derive.

CONTINUATION AFTER CONTRACT EXPIRATION
If a written commission contract expires and Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee nevertheless continue to work under its terms, California law presumes the contract's terms remain in full force and effect until the contract is superseded or the employment relationship is terminated by either party.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In the case of a contract that expires and where the parties nevertheless continue to work under the terms of the expired contract, the contract terms are presumed to remain in full force and effect until the contract is superseded or employment is terminated by either party."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2751(b) (California Legislative Information text), the presumed continuation of an expired contract's terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2751.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. This clause and this document's clause on the signed-copy/signed-receipt requirement both derive from the same statutory subsection, § 2751(b); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNED COPY AND SIGNED RECEIPT
California law requires the employer to give a signed copy of the written commission contract to every employee who is a party to it, and to obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee. The signature and receipt-acknowledgment section of this document is designed to satisfy that requirement for Jordan Lee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The employer shall give a signed copy of the contract to every employee who is a party thereto and shall obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2751(b) (California Legislative Information text), the signed-copy and signed-receipt requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2751.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. Both this clause and this document's clause on continuation after contract expiration derive from the same statutory subsection, § 2751(b); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURE AND RECEIPT ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee acknowledges receiving a signed copy of this Commission Agreement from Acme, Inc. on October 1, 2026, and signs below to provide Acme, Inc. the signed receipt for this contract.

Employee Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: October 1, 2026

Company Representative Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: October 1, 2026
